title: Our five senses: which work from far away, and which need touching

summary.text: You can smell an orange from a few steps away, but you can taste the orange only when it touches your tongue. We have five senses: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching. Each one has its own sense organ: eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin. Your child finds which senses work from across the room and which need touching. They find out that when they smell something, tiny bits of it have floated into their nose.
summary.art: A girl with her eyes shut, taking small steps towards a steel plate with a peeled orange, while her mother walks beside her counting on her fingers.

intro.hook: Close your eyes. Someone in the kitchen is frying mustard seeds and curry leaves. You know it, without seeing a thing. How?
intro.text: Your ears hear the pop of the mustard seeds. Your nose smells the curry leaves. Nobody told you, and you did not look. Your body found out by itself. The ways your body finds out about the world are called your senses. In this unit you test them. You find which senses can tell you about a thing from far away, and which ones need to touch it.
intro.art: A child sitting in a living room with eyes closed and a smile, while in the kitchen behind, a woman tips mustard seeds and curry leaves into a small steel kadai.

outcomes: By the end I can name the five senses and the sense organ for each: eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin.
By the end I can say which senses tell me about a thing from far away (seeing, hearing, smelling) and which need touching (tasting, touching).
By the end I can say that when I smell something, tiny bits of it have floated through the air into my nose.
By the end I can say how one other living being senses the world in their own way.
By the end I can make a guess, test it fairly, and say what I found out.

terms.meaning: A sense is a way your body finds out about the world. Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching are five senses.
terms.example: You hear the pressure cooker whistle with your sense of hearing.
terms.art: A child in the middle of a ring of five small drawings: an eye, an ear, a nose, a tongue and a hand.

terms.meaning: A sense organ is the part of your body that does one sense. Eyes see, ears hear, the nose smells, the tongue tastes, and the skin feels touch.
terms.example: Your nose is the sense organ for smell.
terms.art: A friendly drawing of a child's face with arrows to the eyes, ears, nose and tongue, and one arrow to the skin of the hand.

terms.meaning: A smell is made of tiny bits of a thing that float in the air. When they reach your nose, you smell the thing.
terms.example: When Amma fries banana chips, the smell of coconut oil fills the flat.
terms.art: A plate of banana chips with faint wavy lines rising from it and drifting towards a child's nose.

terms.meaning: Skin covers your whole body. It is the sense organ for touch. It feels if a thing is soft or hard, rough or smooth, warm or cold.
terms.example: Your feet feel that the floor is cold in the morning.
terms.art: A child's bare feet on a cool stone floor, and a hand stroking a soft cotton towel.

explanations.definition: We have five main senses: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching. Each one has a sense organ: eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin.
explanations.description: Your eyes tell you colours and shapes. Your ears tell you sounds. Your nose tells you smells. Your tongue tells you tastes: sweet, sour, salty and bitter. Your skin tells you if a thing is hard or soft, warm or cold. Each sense organ sends messages to your brain, and then you know.
examples: Eating a dosa, you see it is golden, hear it crunch, smell the ghee, taste the salt and feel that it is hot.
Your skin covers all of you, so you can feel a touch on your toes, your back and your nose.
Spinning round and round makes you dizzy. That is your sense of balance, one of your other senses.
explanations.context: This card names the five senses and the body part for each.
explanations.art: A girl eating a crispy dosa on a banana leaf, with five small labels pointing to her eyes, ears, nose, tongue and fingers.

explanations.concept: Some senses reach far, some need touching
explanations.definition: Seeing, hearing and smelling can tell you about a thing far away. Tasting and touching work only when the thing touches you.
explanations.description: Light bounces off a kite into your eyes, so you can see it high in the sky. Sound travels through the air to your ears, so you hear a bell from the next street. Tiny bits of food float through the air to your nose, so you smell cooking in another room. But to taste a mango, the mango must be on your tongue. To feel if a stone is smooth, your skin must touch it.
examples: From the balcony you see a crow on the next building, and hear her caw.
The smell of Onam payasam comes out of the kitchen before anyone brings it to you.
You only know if the payasam is sweet when it is in your mouth.
explanations.context: This card says which senses work from far away, and which need touching. It is what you found in the Smell Steps test.
explanations.art: A child on a balcony: wavy lines of light and sound coming from a crow far away, and a small cloud of smell coming from a kitchen window, while the child's other hand holds a mango to their mouth.

explanations.concept: When you smell a thing, a little of it is in your nose
explanations.definition: A smell is tiny bits of a thing, floating in the air. They are far too small to see. When they reach your nose, you smell the thing.
explanations.description: When you peel an orange, tiny drops of oil spray out of the peel. Tiny bits of that oil float through the air. Some go into your nose when you breathe in. Inside your nose are smell catchers. They catch the bits and send a message to your brain: orange! The closer you are, the more bits reach you. A fan or a breeze carries the bits further.
examples: In the Smell Steps test, you smelled the peeled orange a few steps away, with your eyes shut.
Jasmine in someone's hair can be smelled before they come into the room.
A breeze through the window brings the smell of rain on hot ground.
explanations.context: This card says what a smell really is.
explanations.art: A peeled orange on a plate with tiny dots floating up from the peel and drifting towards a child's nose, with a big circle showing the dots going inside the nose.

explanations.concept: Every living being senses the world in their own way
explanations.description: Humans and other animals all have senses, but not the same ones. A dog can follow the smell of one person's footsteps along a road. An ant smells with her feelers, the two thin threads on her head. A housefly tastes with their feet. A snake flicks out their tongue to pick up smells from the air. Plants sense too. A touch-me-not plant folds their leaves when you touch them. Every living being senses and feels the world. Scientists agree that all these beings sense. They argue about what each one feels.
examples: Ants walk in a line because they follow a smell trail left by other ants.
In 2006, Consuelo De Moraes and her team showed that a climbing plant called dodder grows towards the smell of a tomato plant.
In Mumbai, the scientists Veronica Rodrigues and Obaid Siddiqi studied how fruit flies smell and taste.

perspectives.who: Many biologists who study plants and small animals
perspectives.explanation: Every living being senses and feels. An ant smelling sugar, a dodder plant smelling a tomato and a child smelling an orange are all feeling the world, each in their own way.
Every living being senses. But whether an ant or a plant feels anything like we do is not known. Some of these scientists think feeling needs a brain like ours.

explanations.context: This card is about how other living beings sense. Scientists still argue about what each one feels.
explanations.art: Four small scenes in a row: a dog sniffing a path, an ant touching a sugar grain with her feelers, a fly standing on a sweet, and a touch-me-not plant folding their leaves at a child's finger.

agreed.text: We sense the world through our eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin.
agreed.evidence: When one of these sense organs is covered, that sense stops. Close your eyes and you see nothing. Block your ears and sounds go quiet. Each sense organ sends messages to the brain.

agreed.text: Smells are tiny bits of a thing that float through the air into the nose.
agreed.evidence: A smell is stronger near the thing, and a fan carries it further. Scientists have found smell catchers, called receptors, inside the nose. Each kind catches some kinds of these bits.

agreed.text: Other animals have senses that work differently from ours.
agreed.evidence: Dogs find people by smell, and flies taste with their feet. Scientists have tested these senses again and again.

challenging.claim: People have a poor sense of smell.
challenging.who: A French doctor, Paul Broca, in the 1800s, and many books after him
challenging.for: Dogs can smell many things we miss, and the smell part of the human brain is small compared with the whole brain.
challenging.against: In 2007, blindfolded people followed a chocolate smell trail across a field, sniffing like dogs. People have about 400 kinds of smell catchers and can tell many smells apart.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that people smell poorly.

challenging.claim: You taste sweet only at the tip of your tongue, and bitter only at the back.
challenging.who: A 'tongue map' that was printed in school books for many years
challenging.for: The map came from a German study in 1901, and was copied again and again.
challenging.against: Every part of your tongue that has taste buds can taste sweet, sour, salty and bitter. Put a little sugar on the side of your tongue, and you taste sweet there too.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake: the tongue map.

challenging.who: A very old idea, from the Greek thinker Aristotle
challenging.for: Five senses each have a sense organ you can point to.
challenging.against: We also sense balance, warmth and cold, pain, and where our arms and legs are. Scientists count many more than five.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that there are only five senses.

big_questions.q: You smelled the orange from a few steps away. Is the smell in the orange, or in you?
big_questions.hint: The bits came from the orange. The smell happened when they reached your nose. Can there be a smell with no nose?

big_questions.q: Why can you see the orange from far away, but taste the orange only when it touches you?
big_questions.hint: Think about what travels from the orange to your eyes, and to your nose. Does anything travel to your tongue?

big_questions.q: A dog smells many things we miss. Is the dog's world full of smells we never meet?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a dog does on a walk, and how long the dog sniffs one spot.

big_questions.q: If you could have one new sense, what would you want to find out about the world?
big_questions.hint: Some snakes sense the warmth of a mouse in the dark. Many birds find their way home across the sea. What would you choose?

story.title: Ammamma's Nose
story.note: Kochi is a city in Kerala. Banana chips fried in coconut oil are a Kerala snack. 'Meen' means fish in Malayalam. Ammu, Ammamma, Fatima and Lakshmi are made up.
text: Ammu was six. She lived on the third floor of a block of flats in Kochi, with her grandmother. Everyone called her grandmother Ammamma.
Ammamma's eyes were not strong any more. She saw big shapes and bright colours, but not small things. So Ammamma used her ears, her nose and her hands a lot.
One afternoon, Ammu was drawing on the floor. Ammamma was sitting by the window, folding clothes. Suddenly Ammamma lifted her nose and sniffed.
'Fatima is frying banana chips,' she said. 'In coconut oil.'
Ammu looked up. 'How do you know? Fatima Aunty lives on the ground floor. You can't see her kitchen from here.'
'My nose told me,' said Ammamma. 'Come and smell.'
Ammu sniffed. She smelled nothing. She came to the window and sniffed again. And there it was: warm oil and banana, floating up from below.

Then a pressure cooker whistled next door, once, twice, three times. 'Lakshmi's dal is ready,' said Ammamma. Far away, a woman called out, 'Meen! Meen!' 'And the fish seller is at the gate,' said Ammamma. 'Today she has sardines. I can hear the basket.'
Ammu laughed. 'Ammamma, you know everything that happens in this building, and you don't even look!'
'My ears and my nose look for me,' said Ammamma.
Ammu thought about the chips. 'But how did the smell come all the way up here? Fatima Aunty did not bring it.'

'When the chips fry, tiny bits of them float up into the air,' said Ammamma. 'They are far too small to see. They float out of her window, up to ours, and into your nose. Then your nose says: banana chips!'
Ammu's eyes went very wide. 'So a little bit of Fatima Aunty's banana chips is inside my nose?'
Ammamma laughed until her glasses slipped. 'Yes. A very, very tiny bit.'
Ammu jumped up. 'Let's go and check!'

So they went down the stairs, slowly. Ammamma held the rail with one hand and Ammu's shoulder with the other. On the second floor, the smell was stronger. On the first floor, it was stronger still. At the bottom, it was so strong that Ammu's tummy rumbled.
Fatima Aunty opened her door with a big spoon in her hand. Behind her, chips were frying in a black kadai, popping and fizzing.
'I knew you two would come,' she smiled, and she gave Ammu a warm chip.
Ammu held the chip. It felt warm and hard. She looked at it. It was round and yellow. She bit it, and it went crunch. It tasted salty.
'Ammamma!' said Ammu. 'I used all my senses on one chip. My eyes, my ears, my nose, my tongue and my fingers!'
'And which sense found the chip first?' asked Ammamma.
Ammu thought. 'My nose. From all the way upstairs. My tongue had to wait till the chip was in my mouth.'

At night the lights went out for a while, as they sometimes did in the rain. The flat was dark. But Ammu smelled the jasmine flowers in Ammamma's hair. She knew Ammamma was close, even before Ammamma's hand found hers.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Ammu finds that a smell is tiny bits of a thing that travel to us, so her nose knew about the chips long before her tongue could. She also sees that Ammamma, whose eyes are weak, knows a great deal through her other senses.
ask: How did Ammamma know that Fatima Aunty was frying banana chips?
Why was the smell stronger as they went down the stairs?
Which senses did Ammu use on one chip? Which one found the chip first?
How did Ammu know Ammamma was close in the dark?
art: A grandmother in a cotton sari and big glasses sitting by a window in a Kochi flat, lifting her nose to sniff, while a girl draws on the floor.
A girl and her grandmother walking slowly down a stairwell, the grandmother's hand on the girl's shoulder, with faint wavy lines of smell rising from below.
A smiling woman in a doorway holding a big spoon, with a black kadai of frying banana chips behind her, handing a chip to a girl.
A dark room lit only by a little rain light from the window, a girl reaching towards her grandmother, with jasmine flowers in the grandmother's hair.

games.title: Hop to the Sense: which body part tells you?
games.players: 1 or more players and one caller.
games.context: This is a moving game. Five big sense cards lie on the floor. The caller reads a thing card, and you hop onto the sense that would tell you about that thing.

printables.title: 5 big sense cards for the floor

items.f: A spoon of sugar in your mouth
A crow cawing on the balcony
The smell of rain on hot ground

items.b: All five senses can tell you something

rules: Put the five big sense cards on the floor, a big step apart.
Shuffle the 16 thing cards into a pile. The caller reads the top card out loud.
The player whose turn it is hops onto the sense card that would tell them about that thing.
If more than one sense would tell you, put one foot on one card and one hand on another.
The caller reads the back of the card. If the player found one of the right senses, they get a point.
Players take turns, one card each. When the pile is finished, count the points. The most points wins. If you play alone, try to beat your own points next time.
Then swap: the caller hops, and a player becomes the caller. A grown-up whispers the cards to a caller who cannot read yet.

setup.art: Five large paper cards on a floor in a row, showing an eye, an ear, a nose, a tongue and a hand, with a child standing ready to hop.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the five sense cards on the floor.

setup.art: A child with one foot on the nose card and one hand on the tongue card, while a woman holds up a card with a lemon drawn on it.
setup.caption: 2. Hear the thing, then hop to the sense that tells you about it.

flow.do: 1. Lay the five sense cards on the floor, a big step apart. 2. Read each card to your child.
flow.say: These cards are your five senses. Which part of your body goes with each card?
flow.kid: Look at the five cards. Which part of your body goes with each?

flow.do: 1. Mix the thing cards. 2. Read one at a time. 3. Your child hops onto a sense card. 4. Read the back.
flow.say: A temple bell. Which sense tells you about a bell? Hop onto it!
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Hop onto the sense that tells you.

ask.q: A mango! Which senses can tell you about a mango?
good: Eyes see it is yellow.
Nose smells it.
Tongue tastes it is sweet.
Skin feels it is smooth.
Ears hear the slurp!

flow.parent: Many things use more than one sense. Praise any sense that really works, and ask 'Any more?'

flow.do: Ask the check question. Then let your child be the caller for one round, and you hop.
flow.say: Now you be the caller, and I will hop.
flow.kid: Now you read a card. A grown-up hops.

check.q: A friend whispers a secret to you. Which sense organ do you use?
check.why: Ears hear sounds, and a whisper is a very quiet sound. The tongue tastes and the skin feels touch.

games.title: Guess the Home Sound: ears only
games.players: 2 or more players. One makes the sounds, the others listen.
games.context: This is a listening game. The listener closes their eyes. The sound maker makes a sound from a card, and the listener guesses what made it, using only their ears.

printables.title: 12 sound cards for the sound maker

items.f: Pour water from a jug into a steel tumbler.
Tear a sheet of newspaper slowly.
Stir a spoon round inside a steel tumbler.
Shake a closed dabba with a little rice in it.
Brush your hair with a comb near the listener.
Bite into an apple or a carrot.
Open and shut a zip on a bag.
Bounce a ball on the floor three times.
Put on and take off a bangle or a steel bracelet.

printables.title: Score sheet: tick for a right guess

rules: The listener sits and closes their eyes. With more than two players, everyone except the sound maker listens, and each listener keeps their own score sheet.
The sound maker picks a card, makes that sound once, and asks 'What was that?'
The listener guesses. The sound maker reads the back of the card.

A right guess gets a tick. After the sound maker has made six sounds, put all 12 cards back, shuffle, and swap jobs, so everyone is the sound maker once. With 4 players, that is four turns of six sounds.
At the end, count the ticks. The most ticks wins, or everyone tries to beat their own ticks next time.
A grown-up reads the cards to a sound maker who cannot read yet.

setup.art: A child sitting cross-legged on a mat with eyes closed and a big smile, listening.
setup.caption: 1. The listener closes their eyes.

setup.art: A woman pouring water from a steel jug into a steel tumbler near the listening child.
setup.caption: 2. Make one sound. The listener guesses what made it.

flow.do: Your child sits and closes their eyes. Gather the things for the sound cards.
flow.say: Close your eyes. Your ears are going to do all the work. Ready?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Only your ears can help you now.

flow.do: 1. Make the sound on one card. 2. Ask what it was. 3. Read the back. 4. Tick the score sheet. 5. After six sounds, shuffle the cards and swap jobs.
flow.say: What was that sound? What do you think made it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Listen. What made that sound? Say why you think so.

ask.q: How did you know what made the sound?
good: It sounded splashy, like water.
It was a crunch, like biting an apple.

flow.parent: Ask for the reason, not only the guess. 'It was splashy' is the start of good listening.

flow.do: Talk about which sounds were easy and which were hard.
flow.say: Which sound was hardest to guess? Would it be easier with your eyes open?
flow.kid: Which sound was hard? Would your eyes help?

check.q: The listener's eyes were shut. Which sense organ found the sounds?
check.why: Ears are the sense organ for hearing. The sound travelled through the air to the listener's ears.

experiments.title: Smell Steps: how close must you come to smell an orange?
experiments.context: In this experiment you stand a few steps away from a plate, with your eyes shut. You take one small step at a time, and raise your hand when you smell something. Then you find which of your senses work from far away, and which need touching.
experiments.question: From across the room, which senses can tell you about an orange? How close must you come to smell the orange?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Standing far away, will you see the orange? Hear it? Smell it? Taste it? Feel it? How many steps will you take before you smell it? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every round starts at the same line, with the same small steps and three sniffs at each step. The fan is off and the windows are shut, so moving air does not help one round more than another. In one round the plate is empty. That shows whether you really smell something, or are only guessing.

materials.item: an orange, mosambi or lemon (any fruit with a peel that smells)
2 steel plates, the same kind
a steel spoon
a dupatta or soft cloth to cover the eyes, or just closed eyes
a piece of chalk, a slipper or a line of tape to mark the start line
paper and a pencil for the results

experiments.safety: The child walks with their eyes shut, so clear toys and wires off the floor first. A grown-up walks right beside them.

schedule.what: Guess, look and listen from far away, take smell steps with an empty plate and then with a peeled orange, swap so the grown-up takes the steps too, then touch and taste.

experiments.record: Draw the five sense organs in a row. Under each, draw a tick if it worked from the start line, and a cross if it needed touching. Write how many steps you took before you smelled the orange, and how many the grown-up took. A grown-up helps with the writing.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Smelled nothing, even at the plate
3 small steps (3 steps still to go to the plate)

setup.art: A living room with a steel plate holding a whole orange on a low table, and a chalk line on the floor about six child steps away.
setup.caption: 1. Put the plate on a table. Mark a start line six small steps away.

setup.art: A girl at the chalk line with a dupatta over her eyes, her mother beside her, and a woman at the table peeling an orange over a plate.
setup.caption: 2. Eyes shut. A grown-up peels the orange over the plate.

setup.art: The girl, still with covered eyes, one step from the table with her hand raised high, smiling.
setup.caption: 3. Take one small step at a time. Raise your hand when you smell it.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the fan and shut the windows. 2. Put a whole orange on a steel plate on a low table. 3. Mark a start line six small child steps from the table. 4. Clear the floor between.
flow.say: We are going to test your senses. Here is an orange on a plate. You will stand back here, at this line.
flow.kid: Look at the orange on the plate. Now stand on the start line.
flow.parent: Keep the second plate empty and out of sight in the kitchen. Do not peel the orange yet. Your hands must not smell of orange for the empty round.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess for each sense, from the start line. Write their guesses down.
flow.say: From this line, which of your senses can tell you about the orange? Can you see it? Hear it? Smell it? Taste it? Feel it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. From here, can you see the orange? Hear it? Smell it? Taste it? Feel it? Why?

good: I can see it, because it is in front of me.
I can't taste it, because it is not in my mouth.
Maybe I can smell it, because smells come out of the kitchen.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Do not say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Your child looks at the orange from the line. 2. Tap the plate twice with the steel spoon. 3. Ask about each sense. 4. Tick or cross each one.
flow.say: Can you see the orange from here? Now listen. Did you hear the plate? Can you smell the orange? Can you taste it, or feel it?
flow.kid: Look at the orange. Listen to the spoon. Can you smell it, taste it, or feel it?

ask.q: Which senses worked from the line?
good: My eyes saw it.
My ears heard the spoon on the plate.
I can't smell it yet.

flow.parent: A whole orange gives off little smell, so many children smell nothing from the line. Whatever your child finds is a real result. Tasting and touching need contact, so they get a cross.

flow.do: 1. Your child covers their eyes. 2. Quietly swap the orange for the empty plate, and take the orange to the kitchen. 3. Your child takes one small step at a time, and sniffs three times at each step. 4. Count the steps.
flow.say: Close your eyes. There may be something on the plate, or there may be nothing. Take one small step, and sniff three times. Raise your hand only if you really smell something.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Take one small step. Sniff three times. Hand up only if you smell something.

good: No, nothing.
Maybe a tiny bit of the kitchen.

flow.parent: This is the empty round. Walk right beside your child. If they raise a hand, say 'Tell me what you smell', but do not say the plate is empty until the end.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits on the start line and covers their eyes. 2. In the kitchen, with the door shut, peel the orange by hand. Squeeze a piece of peel over the plate. 3. Wash your hands with soap. 4. Put the plate with the fruit and peel on the table. 5. Your child stands, and does the smell steps again. Count the steps.
flow.say: Eyes closed again. Same as before: one small step, three sniffs. Hand up when you smell something. What do you smell?
flow.kid: Eyes closed. One small step. Sniff three times. Hand up when you smell something.

ask.q: What do you smell? How many steps did you take?
good: Orange!
I smelled it after three steps.
I smelled it straight away, from the line.

flow.parent: Squeezing the peel sprays tiny drops of oil, so the smell gets strong. Many children smell it a few steps from the plate. If your child smells nothing until the plate, squeeze the peel again or move the start line two steps closer, and repeat. If they smell it from the line, that is a real result too. Write the number of steps.

flow.do: 1. Swap jobs. Your child holds the plate with the peeled orange. 2. You stand on the start line with your eyes shut. Take small steps, with three sniffs at each step. 3. Your child counts your steps.
flow.say: Now it is my turn. Count my steps. Who smelled the orange from further away, you or me?
flow.kid: Count the grown-up's steps. Who smelled the orange from further away?

ask.q: Did the grown-up smell the orange at the same place as you?
good: No, the grown-up smelled it sooner.
Yes, we stopped at the same place.

flow.parent: The room already smells of orange after the last round, so you may smell it from the line. That is a real result. Different noses smell at different distances, and that is fine.

flow.do: 1. Your child opens their eyes and comes to the plate. 2. They touch the peel. 3. They taste one piece of the fruit.
flow.say: Now touch the peel. What does it feel like? Now taste one piece. Could you taste it from the line?
flow.kid: Touch the peel. Now taste a piece. Could you taste it from far away?

ask.q: What did your skin and tongue tell you?
good: The peel is bumpy and a bit oily.
It tastes sweet and a bit sour.
I could only taste it when it was in my mouth.

flow.do: Ask what they found, what they saw, and why. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Which senses told you about the orange from far away? Which needed touching? The orange never moved. So how did the smell get to your nose?
flow.kid: Which senses worked from far? Which needed touching? How did the smell reach you?

ask.q: How did the smell get to your nose?
good: Bits of the orange came through the air.
The smell floated to me.

check.q: With your eyes shut, you smelled the orange before you reached the plate. Why?
options: Tiny bits from the orange peel floated through the air into my nose
check.why: Tiny bits from the peel float in the air. When they reach your nose, you smell the orange. Your nose never touched it.

flow.think: When you smell an orange, is a little bit of the orange inside your nose?

activities.title: The Senses Tray: which body part told you?
activities.context: In this activity you explore five things on a tray. For each one, you find out which part of your body told you about it.

materials.item: a tray or a big steel plate
a steel tumbler and a spoon
a few curry leaves, a flower, or a piece of ginger
a small piece of jaggery or a pinch of sugar
a cotton ball or a soft cloth
a bright picture book or a coloured cloth

schedule.what: Explore the tray. Say which body part told you about each thing. Touch each sense organ.

activities.record: Draw one thing from the tray, and draw the body part that told you about it next to it.

setup.art: A steel tray holding a steel tumbler with a spoon, curry leaves, a piece of jaggery, a cotton ball and a bright picture book.
setup.caption: 1. Put five things on a tray.

setup.art: A boy crushing a curry leaf near his nose, with his eyes closed, while his mother points to her own nose.
setup.caption: 2. Explore each thing. Which body part told you?

flow.do: 1. Hand your child one thing at a time. 2. Let them explore it however they like. 3. Ask what they found out, and which body part told them.
flow.say: Here is a tumbler and a spoon. Find out about it. What did you find? Which part of you told you that?
flow.kid: Find out about each thing. Which part of you told you?

ask.q: What did you find out about the curry leaf?
good: It smells strong when I crush it. My nose told me.
It is green. My eyes told me.
It is smooth. My fingers told me.

flow.parent: Let your child choose how to explore. Some will bang the tumbler, some will sniff it. Afterwards, name the sense they used.

flow.do: Play 'Touch your…': call out a sense, and your child touches its sense organ.
flow.say: Touch the part that sees. The part that hears. The part that smells. The part that tastes. Now the part that feels a touch.
flow.kid: Touch the part that sees. Now hears. Now smells. Now tastes. Now feels.

check.q: Which sense organ told you that the jaggery is sweet?
check.why: The tongue tastes sweet, sour, salty and bitter. Eyes can see the jaggery is brown, but only the tongue tastes the sweet.

flow.parent: For touch, many children point to their hands. Tell them that the skin all over the body feels touch, even the skin on their back and feet.

activities.title: Lights Out: which senses still work in the dark?
activities.context: In this activity you sit in a dark room for a short while with a grown-up. You find out which senses stop working in the dark, and which keep going.

materials.item: a room you can make dark, by switching off the lights and closing the curtains, in the evening
a torch or a phone light
something with a smell, such as a cut lemon or a flower
a steel tumbler and a spoon

schedule.what: Sit in the dark. Test each sense. Switch on the torch and talk about what changed.

activities.record: Draw a dark room. Draw the senses that still worked in the dark inside it.

setup.art: A woman and a girl sitting on a mattress in a dim room in the evening, the woman holding a torch that is switched off.
setup.caption: 1. Sit together. Switch off the light.

setup.art: In the dark room, the girl holding a cut lemon to her nose while the woman taps a steel tumbler with a spoon.
setup.caption: 2. Test each sense in the dark.

flow.do: 1. Sit with your child on the floor or a bed. 2. Close the curtains and switch off the lights.
flow.say: Let's sit together in the dark. I am right here. What can you see now?
flow.kid: Sit with your grown-up. The light goes off. What can you see?

flow.do: 1. Tap the tumbler. 2. Hold the lemon near your child's nose. 3. Put your hand gently on their arm. 4. Ask about each sense.
flow.say: Can you hear the tumbler? Can you smell the lemon? Can you feel my hand on your arm? Which senses still work in the dark?
flow.kid: Listen. Smell. Feel. Which senses still work in the dark?

ask.q: Which sense stopped in the dark?
good: Seeing. I can't see anything.
My eyes don't work in the dark.

flow.do: Switch on the torch. Ask why seeing came back.
flow.say: Now the torch is on. You can see again. Your eyes did not change. What changed?
flow.kid: The torch is on. You can see again. What changed?

good: Because there is light.
Eyes need light to see.

check.q: In the dark, which sense stops working?
check.why: Eyes need light to see. In the dark, no light reaches your eyes. Ears, nose, tongue and skin still work.

flow.parent: Your eyes are not switched off in the dark. They need light coming from things to see them. With no light, there is nothing for them to catch.

activities.title: Touch Words: rough, smooth, soft, hard, warm, cold
activities.context: In this activity you feel things from around the home and sort them by what your skin tells you.

materials.item: 6 to 8 home things, such as a steel spoon, a towel, a comb, a coconut scrubber or a rough brush, a cotton ball, a stone or a tile, a banana
a steel tumbler of lukewarm water (not hot), to feel warm
a dupatta or cloth to cover the eyes
paper and crayons

schedule.what: Feel each thing with eyes covered. Say a touch word. Sort the things into groups.

activities.record: Draw two groups: things that felt rough and things that felt smooth.

setup.art: A row of home things on a mat: a steel spoon, a folded towel, a comb, a coconut scrubber, a cotton ball and a banana.
setup.caption: 1. Put the things in a row.

setup.art: A girl with covered eyes stroking a coconut scrubber, with a woman beside her holding the next thing.
setup.caption: 2. Feel each one with eyes covered. Say a touch word.

flow.do: 1. Cover your child's eyes. 2. Put one thing in their hands at a time. 3. Ask for a touch word: rough, smooth, soft, hard, warm or cold.
flow.say: Feel this. What does your skin tell you? Is it rough or smooth? Soft or hard? Warm or cold?
flow.kid: Feel it. Is it rough or smooth? Soft or hard? Warm or cold?

ask.q: What does the steel spoon feel like?
good: Smooth and hard.
Cold.

flow.parent: Steel often feels colder than cloth, though both are in the same room. Your child may notice this. You do not need to explain it now.

flow.do: 1. Uncover the eyes. 2. Sort the things into a rough group and a smooth group, then a soft group and a hard group.
flow.say: Let's sort them. Put everything that felt rough here, and everything smooth there. Now try soft and hard.
flow.kid: Sort them. Rough here. Smooth there. Now soft and hard.

check.why: A cotton ball squashes when you press it, so it feels soft. A spoon and a stone are hard.

activities.title: Shaker Pairs: match them with your ears
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up fills closed boxes with different things, two of each. You shake them and find the pairs, using only your ears.

materials.item: 6 small closed boxes or bottles that look the same, such as empty medicine bottles, small dabbas or paper cups taped shut
2 spoons of rice, 2 spoons of salt, and 8 to 10 rajma or chana

schedule.what: A grown-up fills the boxes. Shake them and find the three pairs. Then open them to check.

activities.record: Draw the three pairs you found, and what was inside each.

setup.art: A woman filling six small identical bottles: two with rice, two with salt, two with a few rajma beans.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up fills two boxes with each thing and closes them.

setup.art: A child holding a small bottle to each ear and shaking them, with four more bottles on the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Shake and listen. Find the two that sound the same.

flow.do: 1. Out of sight, fill two boxes with rice, two with salt and two with a few rajma. 2. Close them tightly. 3. Mix them up on the floor.
flow.say: These boxes all look the same. But inside, two and two are the same. Can your ears find the pairs?
flow.kid: The boxes look the same. Shake them. Can your ears find the pairs?

flow.do: Your child shakes the boxes and puts them in pairs.
flow.say: Shake this one. Now that one. Do they sound the same? What do you think is inside? Why?
flow.kid: Shake two boxes. Do they sound the same? What is inside?

ask.q: What do you think is in this one? Why?
good: Big things, because it goes clonk clonk.
Tiny things, because it sounds like sand.

flow.parent: Rice and salt can sound alike. If your child mixes them up, that is part of the game. Open the boxes to check.

flow.do: Open the boxes and check.
flow.say: Let's open them. Did your ears get it right?
flow.kid: Open the boxes. Were your ears right?

check.q: Your eyes could not see inside the boxes. How did you find the pairs?
check.why: The boxes were closed, so only the sound came out. Big rajma clonk, rice rattles, and salt makes a soft hiss.

activities.safety: Close the boxes tightly, with tape if needed, so nothing spills or goes into little mouths.

projects.title: My Five Senses Book: one sense each day
projects.context: In this project you make a small book with five pages, one for each sense. Each day, you find one thing that you sensed and draw it.

materials.item: 3 sheets of paper, folded in half and stapled or tied with thread to make a small book
crayons or colour pencils

schedule.what: Make the book. Draw something you saw today on the 'Eyes' page.
Draw something you heard on the 'Ears' page.
Draw something you smelled on the 'Nose' page.
Draw something you tasted on the 'Tongue' page.
Draw something you touched on the 'Skin' page. Tell the whole book to someone.

projects.record: The finished book, with one drawing for each sense.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper folded and tied with a thread into a little book, with 'My Senses' on the cover.
setup.caption: 1. Fold and tie three sheets into a book.

setup.art: An open little book showing a drawing of a temple bell on the 'Ears' page.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, draw one thing for one sense.

flow.do: 1. Fold and tie the book. 2. Write 'My Senses' on the cover. 3. Write one sense at the top of each page: Eyes, Ears, Nose, Tongue, Skin. Your child writes what they can, and you write the rest.
flow.say: Each day this week, you will catch one thing with one sense, and draw it. Today is the eyes day. What did you see today that you liked?
flow.kid: Make your book. Today, draw something you saw.

flow.do: Each day, help your child choose one thing for that day's sense and draw it.
flow.say: Today is the ears day. What did you hear today? Was it loud or soft? Where did it come from?
flow.kid: Today, draw something you heard. Was it loud or soft?
flow.wait: Do the next page tomorrow, and the next each day after that.

flow.do: On the nose day, ask where the smell came from.
flow.say: What did you smell today? Were you near it, or far away when you smelled it?
flow.kid: Draw something you smelled. Were you near or far?

flow.do: On the tongue day, ask about tastes.
flow.say: Was the taste sweet, sour, salty or bitter? Draw it.
flow.kid: Draw something you tasted. Say a word for the taste.

flow.do: On the last day, your child draws something they touched on the Skin page. Then they tell the whole book to someone at home.
flow.say: What did you touch today? Was it rough, smooth, soft or hard? Now show your book to someone at home. Which page do you like best?
flow.kid: Draw something you touched. Then show your book to someone and tell them each page.

check.q: Which page of your book could have a drawing of jasmine flowers?
check.why: Jasmine has a strong sweet smell, so the nose page is a good fit. The eyes page could have them too, because jasmine is white and pretty.

challenges.title: A Doorbell for a Neighbour Who Cannot Hear
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A neighbour cannot hear the doorbell. You design a way for her to know someone is at the door, using a different sense.
challenges.problem: A neighbour of yours cannot hear any sounds. When someone rings her doorbell, she does not know. How could you let her know someone is at the door, using her eyes, her nose or her skin?
constraints: It must not need her to hear anything.
A child must be able to use it, or set it going.
Keep string off the floor where people walk, so nobody trips.
materials: string, a ribbon or a dupatta
general: Many homes with someone who cannot hear have a doorbell that flashes a light.
Some people wear a band on the wrist that shakes when the bell rings.
Someone can tap her gently on the shoulder.
creative: She holds one end of a long string. Someone at the door tugs the other end, and she feels it in her hand.
Flash a torch on the wall where she sits.
Wave a bright cloth through the doorway.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your own doorbell for your neighbour. Then try it out at home: one person is the neighbour, and one person comes to the door.

setup.art: An older woman reading in a chair while, far away, a hand presses a doorbell by the front door.
setup.caption: 1. She cannot hear the bell. What else could tell her?

setup.art: A long bright ribbon tied from a door handle to a chair, wiggling, and the older woman looking up and smiling.
setup.caption: 2. Design and test a doorbell for another sense.

flow.do: Read the problem to your child.
flow.say: A neighbour cannot hear. When her doorbell rings, she does not know someone is there. Which other senses could tell her?
flow.kid: A neighbour cannot hear the bell. Which other sense could tell her?

good: Her eyes, if a light flashes.
Her skin, if something touches her.
Her nose? That would be hard!

flow.do: Your child draws one or two ideas. Talk about each one.
flow.say: Draw your idea. Which sense does it use? How would she know it is the door, and not something else?
flow.kid: Draw your doorbell. Which sense does it use?

flow.do: Try the best idea at home. One person plays the neighbour, sitting with their ears covered.
flow.say: Let's test it. You come to the door and use your doorbell. I'll be the neighbour, with my hands over my ears.
flow.kid: Test it. Did the neighbour know someone was at the door?

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Did it work? What would you change?
flow.kid: Did it work? What would you change?

check.q: A doorbell that flashes a light uses which sense?
check.why: A flashing light reaches the eyes, so it uses seeing. It works for someone who cannot hear.

items.p: Here is a child's face and hand. Write or say the sense for each part: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting or touching.
items.why: Each sense organ does one sense. The skin of the hand, and the skin all over the body, does touching.
items.art: A simple drawing of a child's face with the tongue poking out, and one hand, with an empty label next to the eye, ear, nose, tongue and hand.

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to the sense organ that tells you about it.
items.why: Ears hear the bell, eyes see the colour red, the tongue tastes salt, and the skin feels that the towel is soft.
items.art: A bell, a red hibiscus flower, a few chips and a folded towel on the left, and an ear, an eye, a tongue and a hand on the right, mixed up.

items.p: From across the room, can this sense tell you about a thing? Circle the far senses in green, and the touching senses in red.
items.why: Light, sound and tiny smell bits travel through the air to your eyes, ears and nose. To taste or feel a thing, it must touch your tongue or skin.

items.p: In the Smell Steps test, you walked towards a peeled orange with your eyes shut. Draw where you were when you first smelled the orange.
items.a: A drawing of the child a few steps from the plate, with their hand raised.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the child still some steps away from the plate. The smell reached them before they touched the orange.
items.art: A blank box with a small plate drawn at one end.

items.p: Your eyes need light to see.
items.why: True. In a dark room you cannot see, though your eyes are open. When the light comes back, you see again.

items.p: You can feel a touch on your back, not only on your hands.
items.why: True. Skin covers your whole body, so you can feel a touch on your back, your feet and your nose too.

items.p: Three of these are sense organs. Which one is not?
items.why: The nose, ears and tongue are sense organs. The knee helps your leg bend, but it is not a sense organ for one of the five senses.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: how did the smell of the orange get to your nose, when your nose never touched the orange?
items.a: Tiny bits from the orange peel floated through the air and went into my nose.
items.why: A strong answer says that something from the orange travelled through the air to the nose.

items.p: Riya, a girl in Class 1, closes her eyes. Someone pours water into a tumbler. Which sense tells Riya what they did?
items.why: The water makes a splashing sound. The sound travels to Riya's ears.

items.p: Meenakshi and her friend Deepa are smelling jasmine flowers in a garden in Madurai.

views.says: The smell is in the flowers. My nose just finds it.
The smell is in my nose. Tiny bits came from the flowers into my nose, and then I smelled them.

items.ask: Say who you agree with and why, and a grown-up writes it down. Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one side and gives a reason. For Deepa: the bits travelled into my nose, and I smelled them only when they arrived. For Meenakshi: the bits came from the flowers, and they smell like jasmine because of the flowers.
items.why: Both girls are partly right. The tiny bits come from the flowers, but the smell happens when they reach a nose. Scientists and thinkers still talk about where a smell really is.

items.p: Draw your favourite food. Around it, draw each sense organ that can tell you something about it.
items.a: A food with several sense organs drawn around it, such as an eye, a nose and a tongue.
items.why: A strong drawing has more than one sense organ, because most foods can be seen, smelled, tasted and touched, and some can be heard.
items.art: A blank box with a plate drawn in the middle.

items.p: Sowmya says: 'I can only smell a dosa if I can see it.' Is she right? Say what you think, and tell about a time you smelled food you could not see. A grown-up writes it down.
items.a: No. Tiny bits of the dosa float through the air to your nose, so you can smell it from another room.
items.why: A strong answer says that smell travels through the air, so the thing does not have to be in sight.

items.p: If the fan is on, the smell of the orange may reach you faster.
items.why: True. Moving air carries the tiny smell bits further and faster. That is why we kept the fan off, so every round was the same.

items.p: Which sense would tell you first? Sort each one.
items: A pressure cooker whistling in the kitchen
Dosa burning on the tawa in the next room
A friend calling your name from the next flat
Sambar cooking while you are in the bedroom
items.why: Things you cannot see from where you are reach you as sounds or smells. A rainbow makes no sound or smell, so only your eyes find it.

items.p: A dog can tell where a person walked, even after the person has gone.
items.why: True. A person leaves tiny smell bits on the ground, and a dog's nose can follow them.

items.p: In the story 'Ammamma's Nose', Ammu's grandmother cannot see small things. Say what other things Ammamma used to know what was happening in the building, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: She used her ears and her nose: the cooker whistle, the fish seller's basket and the smell of banana chips.
items.why: A strong answer names the ears and the nose, and says what each one told her.

items.p: Draw a line from each living being to how they sense.
pairs: feels touch and folds their leaves
items.why: Every living being senses the world, but in their own way. These are real ways that each one senses.
items.art: An ant, a fly, a snake and a touch-me-not plant on the left, and four short sentences on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Draw an ant walking to a grain of sugar. Draw the smell trail she follows, and the feelers she smells with.
items.a: An ant with two feelers on her head, a trail of tiny dots on the ground, and a sugar grain at the end.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the feelers on the ant's head and the smell trail on the ground that leads her to the sugar.
items.art: A blank box with a grain of sugar drawn at one end.

items.p: Here is a dosa on a plate. Say what each sense tells you about the dosa, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.why: One dosa gives every sense something. Each sense organ tells you something different about the same dosa.
items.art: A dosa on a plate with five empty labels around it: Eyes, Ears, Nose, Tongue, Skin.

items.p: Nirmala and her brother Farhan are talking about dogs in Hyderabad.

views.says: Dogs are better than people at smelling. Our noses are weak.
Dogs are better at some smells. But people are good at smelling too. People can even follow a smell trail.

items.ask: Say who you agree with and why, and a grown-up writes it down. Then say one thing the other one has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence: people followed a chocolate smell trail across a field, so human noses are good. Farhan is right that dogs smell many things we miss.
items.why: For a long time people said human noses are weak. Tests now show humans are good at many smells, while dogs are better at others.

items.p: Name one smell that told you something today, and say what it told you. A grown-up writes it down.
items.a: I smelled toast burning, so I told Amma.
items.why: A strong answer names a real smell and what the child knew from it, such as food being ready or something burning.

videos.title: A short film of people following a scent trail, from the 2007 Berkeley study
videos.why: Shows blindfolded people sniffing their way along a chocolate smell trail across grass, like dogs.
videos.check: Find a real clip of the 2007 human scent-tracking study by Jess Porter, Noam Sobel and colleagues, or a news report showing it.

videos.title: A touch-me-not (Mimosa pudica) plant folding their leaves when touched
videos.why: Shows that plants sense touch too: the leaves fold within a few seconds of a finger touching them.
videos.check: Find a real, unedited clip, not sped up without saying so.

videos.title: A snake flicking their tongue to smell
videos.why: Shows a snake picking up smells from the air with the tongue, a sense very different from ours.
videos.check: Find a clip from a nature programme or a zoo that explains the tongue flick correctly.

quiz.p: Which sense organ do you use to hear?
quiz.why: Ears are the sense organ for hearing. Sound travels through the air into them.

quiz.p: Which one is the sense organ for touch?
quiz.why: Skin covers your whole body and feels touch: rough, smooth, soft, hard, warm and cold.

quiz.p: Which one is NOT one of the five senses?
quiz.why: Jumping is something your body does. Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching are the five senses.

quiz.p: Standing far away from a plate of jalebis, which of these can you NOT do?
quiz.why: You can see and smell from far away. To taste, the jalebi must be on your tongue.

quiz.p: Which two senses need the thing to touch you?
quiz.why: Tasting needs the food on your tongue, and touching needs the thing on your skin. Seeing, hearing and smelling work from far away.

quiz.p: Thenmozhi smells sambar from her bedroom. What reached her nose?
opts: Tiny bits from the sambar, floating in the air
quiz.why: Tiny bits from the hot sambar float through the air. When they reach her nose, she smells sambar.

quiz.p: Why is the smell of a peeled orange stronger when you are close to the plate?
opts: More tiny smell bits reach your nose
quiz.why: Near the plate there are more of the tiny bits in the air, so more of them go into your nose.

opts: Ants have no sense of smell
quiz.why: An ant smells with the two feelers on her head. That is how ants follow a smell trail to food.

quiz.p: A touch-me-not plant folds their leaves when you touch them. What does that show?
quiz.why: The leaves fold right after a touch, so the plant sensed the touch and answered.

quiz.p: Gauri in Pune tests her nose: one plate has an orange, one plate is empty. Why the empty plate?
opts: To check she is not just guessing
To count how many steps she takes
To make the room smell nice
quiz.why: If Gauri smells nothing at the empty plate, then the smell she finds at the other plate really came from the orange. That makes the test fair.

quiz.p: Why does every round of the Smell Steps test start at the same line?
opts: So the rounds are fair to compare
quiz.why: If every round starts at the same line, a different number of steps means a different distance. That makes the test fair.

applications: Cooks smell and taste food as they cook, to know when it is ready.
Gas companies add a strong smell to cooking gas, so people can smell a leak and stay safe.
Doctors often check a baby's eyes and ears soon after birth, to make sure the senses work.
Police dogs follow the smell of a lost person to find them.

spotted.text: The smell of filter coffee drifting out of a kitchen in Chennai in the morning, before anyone says it is ready.
spotted.art: A steel filter coffee set on a kitchen counter with faint wavy lines of smell drifting towards a doorway.

spotted.text: Jasmine flowers in a woman's hair on a crowded bus in Madurai, smelled before she is seen.
spotted.art: A crowded bus with a woman wearing a string of jasmine in her plait, and a child nearby lifting her nose.

spotted.text: A street dog in Kolkata sniffing every corner on the walk, finding out who passed by.
spotted.art: A street dog with their nose to the ground at a street corner, under a yellow taxi.

spotted.text: A line of ants marching to a drop of jaggery on the kitchen floor, following a smell trail.
spotted.art: A neat line of small black ants on a kitchen floor leading to a drop of jaggery syrup.

spotted.text: A touch-me-not plant at the edge of a footpath, folding their leaves when a child's finger touches them.
spotted.art: A child's finger touching a touch-me-not plant, the touched leaves folding up.

open_questions.q: How many different smells can people tell apart?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists say thousands, and one study in 2014 said more than a trillion. Other scientists say that study's maths was wrong. Nobody knows the number yet.

open_questions.q: Why can one smell bring back an old memory so strongly?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that smell messages reach the parts of the brain that keep memories and feelings. But how a smell brings back a whole day from long ago is not fully known.

open_questions.q: What does the world feel like to an ant, a dog or a plant?
open_questions.why_open: We can test what other beings sense by watching what they do. But nobody can feel another being's world from the inside.

ask_kids: What can you smell right now? Where is it coming from?
Which sense told you first that food was ready today?
Close your eyes. How many sounds can you hear?
What does the floor feel like under your feet?
If you were an ant, how would you find the sugar?
Which sense would you miss most? Why?

jokes.j: What did one eye say to the other eye?
jokes.a: Between you and me, something smells!

jokes.j: Why is your nose in the middle of your face?
Why did the orange stop in the middle of the road?
What has ears but cannot hear?
What has a tongue but cannot talk?
What has an eye but cannot see?
What has teeth but cannot bite?
What has hands but cannot clap?
What did the jasmine say to the nose?

maths.problem: In the Smell Steps test, Nila smelled the orange after 3 small steps. Her brother Sai smelled the orange after 5 small steps. Both started at the same line. Who smelled the orange from further away?
maths.answer: Nila. She took fewer steps, so she was further from the plate.
maths.explain: Both started at the same line. Fewer steps means you stopped further from the plate. 3 is less than 5, so Nila was further away when the smell reached her.
maths.context: This is about the Smell Steps test, where you walked towards a peeled orange with your eyes shut.
maths.why_maths: Counting steps turns 'near' and 'far' into numbers we can compare.

maths.problem: You eat a crunchy dosa. You see it, hear it crunch, smell it, taste it and feel that it is hot. How many senses did you use?
maths.explain: Count one finger for each sense: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching. That is 5.
maths.context: This is about using all your senses on one food.
maths.why_maths: Counting the senses shows that one food can give every sense something to find.

maths.problem: In the Guess the Home Sound game, Bornali heard 6 sounds. She guessed 4 right. How many did she guess wrong?
maths.explain: 6 sounds take away 4 right guesses leaves 2. So 2 sounds were hard for her ears.
maths.context: This is about the listening game, where you closed your eyes and guessed what made each sound.
maths.why_maths: Taking away shows how many sounds were hard, so you know which ones to listen to again.

song.title: Eyes and Ears and Nose
song.note: Topic-level song for Senses and perception L1

links.title: StoryWeaver, free picture books from Pratham Books
links.why: For the parent: free picture books in many Indian languages to read aloud. Search for books about the senses, smells and sounds.

links.title: Nehru Science Centre
links.why: A science centre with hands-on galleries, good for a family day out.

links.title: Visvesvaraya Industrial and Technological Museum
links.why: A science museum with hands-on exhibits and a children's section.

warmup.q: How many main senses do we have?
warmup.a: Five: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.

warmup.q: Can you taste a mango from across the room?
warmup.a: No. You taste the mango only when it is on your tongue.

warmup.q: What does a smell travel through to reach you?
Which sense stops working in the dark?

founder: ideas/by_topic/senses.md: the Grade 1 reality grid ('what's real is what we see, touch, hear'), used in the big question on whether the smell is in the orange or in you, and the Obaid Siddiqi card (fruit flies and the genetics of taste and smell), used in the explanation on other living beings. The Ibn al-Haytham card fits the light units better, and the electricity safety activities do not fit this topic. The Level 3 unit uses the nose-pinch flavour test, the two-point test, the mystery bag and Kim's game, so this unit uses smell steps, a senses tray, a dark room and shaker pairs instead.
science: Jess Porter, Noam Sobel and colleagues, 'Mechanisms of scent-tracking in humans', Nature Neuroscience 10 (2007): blindfolded people followed a chocolate scent trail across a field and improved with practice.
John McGann, 'Poor human olfaction is a 19th-century myth', Science 356 (2017): traces the idea of a weak human nose to Paul Broca.
Linda Buck and Richard Axel, Cell 65 (1991): the family of genes for smell receptors. Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 2004.
Justin Runyon, Mark Mescher and Consuelo De Moraes, Science 313 (2006): dodder seedlings grow towards the smell of tomato plants.
The 'tongue map' came from a misreading of David Hänig's 1901 study of taste sensitivity. All tastes are sensed across the tongue.
Caroline Bushdid and colleagues, Science 343 (2014): estimate that people can tell apart over a trillion smells, later disputed by Richard Gerkin and Jason Castro (2015) and Markus Meister (2015).

roots.context: We have tested our five senses, and found which ones reach far and which need touching. Now we ask what the Smell Steps test tells us about us and the world.

deep_truth.truth: With your eyes shut, you smelled the orange a few steps away, before you touched it. Tiny bits of the peel had floated through the air into your nose. Your tongue could taste the orange only by touching it. So when you smell something, a little of that thing has already reached you.
deep_truth.habit: We think of smelling like looking: the thing stays over there, and we notice it from here. But the test shows that bits of the orange travel and come into us. Smelling happens where the orange and your body meet.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Smell Steps test, with eyes shut, the child smelled nothing at the empty plate, then smelled the peeled orange before reaching the plate. Taste came only when the orange touched the tongue.

three.who_am_i: You are a body full of senses. Your eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin bring the world to you all day.
three.what_is_life: Every living being senses the world. An ant smells with her feelers, and a plant feels a touch.
three.what_is_this_world: Light goes to your eyes, sound goes to your ears, and tiny bits of things go to your nose.

roots.thread: You stand across the room from an orange, and still you smell it. Tiny bits of the orange float through the air into your nose. Light and sound also reach you from far away. Every being meets the world through their own senses, and what each one senses is different.

teachings.teaching: A teacher, Uddalaka, asks his son to put salt in water overnight. In the morning the salt cannot be seen. But when the son sips from the top, the middle and the bottom, the water is salty everywhere.
teachings.link: Your eyes could not see the salt, but your tongue found it. In the Smell Steps test, your eyes could not see the bits of orange in the air, but your nose found them.

teachings.source: Kabir, a doha often quoted as 'Kasturi kundal basai'
teachings.teaching: The musk deer smells the sweet smell of musk and runs through the forest looking for it. But the musk is in the deer's own body.
teachings.link: In the poem, the deer follows a smell. A real smell is also tiny bits of a thing carried by the air, as you found with the orange.

teachings.source: Buddhist teaching of the six sense bases (Salayatana Samyutta, Samyutta Nikaya 35)
teachings.teaching: The Buddha spoke of six senses: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the mind, which knows thoughts.
teachings.link: We found five senses with sense organs. This teaching adds the mind as a sixth sense, which knows what the other five bring.

science.text: A smell is made of tiny particles, called molecules, that float from a thing through the air. Smell catchers in the nose, called receptors, catch them.
How many smells people can tell apart is still argued about. Guesses go from thousands to more than a trillion.

other_view.view: The tiny bits from the orange are only chemicals. They have no smell until a nose and a brain meet them. So for these scientists, the smell of orange is made inside you, not in the orange.

practice.title: One slow sniff
practice.say: Hold a curry leaf or a piece of orange peel. Close your eyes. Breathe out slowly. Now breathe in slowly through your nose, and feel the smell come in. Breathe out. Do it two more times. Tiny bits of the leaf are now inside your nose.
practice.kid: Hold a leaf. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly through your nose. Feel the smell come in. A little of the leaf is now in you.

ask: When you smell the ground after rain, is a little of the ground inside your nose?
If you smell jasmine in a friend's hair, what has travelled from her hair to you?
What would the world be like if you could smell as well as a dog?
roots.art: A girl with her eyes closed, holding a curry leaf near her nose, with tiny faint dots drifting from the leaf towards her as she breathes in.

how_we_found_out.story: In the late 1800s, a French doctor named Paul Broca studied the brains of humans and other animals. He saw that the part of the human brain used for smell is small next to the rest of the brain. So he put humans in a group of animals with a weak sense of smell. For more than a hundred years, books repeated that people smell poorly. In 2007, scientists at the University of California, Berkeley, tested this. They laid a trail of chocolate smell across a grassy field. People wore blindfolds and earmuffs, and crawled with their noses near the ground, like dogs. Most of them followed the trail, and they got faster with practice. In 2017, the scientist John McGann looked at all the evidence and called the weak human nose a myth. Earlier, in 1991, Linda Buck and Richard Axel had found the genes for the smell catchers inside the nose. Humans have about 400 kinds. Buck and Axel won the Nobel Prize for this in 2004.
how_we_found_out.who: Paul Broca, a French doctor; a team at the University of California, Berkeley; John McGann, an American brain scientist; Linda Buck and Richard Axel, American scientists
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People have a poor sense of smell.

playtest: Walked through the unit as a parent and a child in a flat, step by step. Minutes and schedules agree, the Smell Steps test is fair (same line, empty-plate round, fan off) and says honestly what a child may or may not smell. Fixed: the sound game ran out of cards with 4 players, so cards are now put back and shuffled for each sound maker; the project wait line no longer repeats the day steps; a worksheet drawing that repeated the smell-travel idea is now about an ant's trail; one silly quiz option is replaced. The three video ids are still to be found.
